passage: I'm Sahil. When Rehana admitted she had pushed a change without testing and broken the build, I could see her bracing. So I told her about the worst project of my early career: a billing module I insisted on rewriting alone, then hid my delays for weeks, and shipped late with bugs that cost a client an evening of manual work. I kept it to three minutes, no dramatic ending, because this wasn't my moment. What I learned, I said, was that telling the team early would have saved everyone time. Then I turned it back to her: 'What would you want the team to know about yesterday?' Rehana let out a breath and began to explain. Later she said it was easier to talk once she knew I had stumbled too.

qa.q: How long did Sahil's story take?
qa.a: Sahil kept it to three minutes.

qa.q: What did Sahil want to make sure of while telling the story?
qa.a: Sahil was concerned that Rehana was bracing herself, so Sahil kept the story short and turned it back to her, making sure the talk stayed about her.

qa.q: What could Sahil do if Rehana still stayed quiet about the mistake?
qa.a: Sahil could offer to go through the change together on a shared screen, since working side by side takes away some of the pressure of explaining.

qa.q: How did the story feel to Rehana?
qa.a: Rehana felt relieved and safer: she let out a breath, and later said it was easier to talk knowing Sahil had stumbled too. 🙂

grounding: Shows a mentor telling a short honest story of a past bad project and its lesson so the mentee can admit a mistake, without making the story about themselves.
